entity.name: Tiberius
entity.description: The reluctant emperor Pliny called the gloomiest of men. Rome's second emperor and one of its greatest generals, Tiberius conquered Pannonia and Dalmatia before inheriting a throne he never wanted. Forced to divorce the wife he loved, he retreated to Capri and ruled by letter for the last decade of his reign.

story.name: Tiberius
story.description: Forced to divorce his beloved wife, self-exiled to Rhodes, made emperor by default after every heir died, then retreated to Capri. Rome's gloomiest ruler and most capable general.

moments.name: Tiberius Is Born into Rome's Ancient Claudian Family
moments.subtitle: His mother Livia will soon divorce his father to marry the future Emperor Augustus
moments.description: On November 16, 42 BC, Tiberius Julius Caesar Augustus was born in Rome to Tiberius Claudius Nero and Livia Drusilla, both members of the ancient patrician gens Claudia. Within four years, Livia would divorce his father and marry Octavian, the future Emperor Augustus, upending young Tiberius's family life. At age nine, Tiberius delivered the eulogy for his biological father at the rostra. This boy from one of Rome's oldest families would become one of its most successful generals and its most reluctant emperor.

moments.name: Tiberius Abandons Rome and Retires to Rhodes
moments.subtitle: Married to a woman he loathes and forbidden from seeing the one he loves
moments.description: In 6 BC, while on the verge of becoming the second most powerful man in Rome, Tiberius stunned the empire by announcing his withdrawal from politics and sailing to Rhodes. Augustus had forced Tiberius to divorce his beloved wife Vipsania and marry Julia, Augustus's promiscuous daughter. According to Suetonius, when Tiberius once ran into Vipsania, he followed her home crying. Now married to a woman he despised, publicly humiliated by her escapades, Tiberius chose self-exile over power. Augustus begged him to stay. Tiberius anchored off Ostia until he heard Augustus had survived an illness, then sailed away.

moments.name: Tiberius Becomes Rome's Second Emperor at Age 55
moments.subtitle: Every other heir has died; the reluctant general finally accepts the throne
moments.description: On August 19, AD 14, Emperor Augustus died, and Tiberius became princeps of the Roman Empire at the age of 55. He was never Augustus's first choice. Augustus's grandsons Gaius and Lucius had been preferred, but Lucius died in AD 2 and Gaius was killed in Armenia in AD 4. Only then did Augustus formally adopt Tiberius as his heir. Ancient sources describe Tiberius as accepting the role with great reluctance, perhaps feeling genuinely inadequate compared to the charismatic Augustus. Pliny the Elder would later call him the gloomiest of men, yet Tiberius proved an effective and fiscally responsible administrator.

moments.name: Tiberius Orders His Powerful Prefect Sejanus Executed for Treason
moments.subtitle: Ruling from Capri by letter, the reclusive emperor destroys the man who ran Rome
moments.description: In AD 31, Emperor Tiberius ordered the execution of Sejanus, his praetorian prefect who had amassed enormous power while Tiberius governed from the island of Capri. After the deaths of his nephew Germanicus in AD 19 and his son Drusus in AD 23, Tiberius had become reclusive, leaving Rome in AD 26 and entrusting daily governance to the ambitious Sejanus. When Tiberius discovered Sejanus was plotting to seize the throne, he orchestrated his downfall by letter from Capri. The episode illustrates both Tiberius's paranoia and his capacity for decisive action even in isolation.

moments.name: Tiberius Dies at 77, Succeeded by His Grand-Nephew Caligula
moments.subtitle: The gloomiest of men leaves behind a full treasury that Caligula will drain
moments.description: On March 16, AD 37, Emperor Tiberius died at the age of 77, likely at his villa on Capri or nearby Misenum. He had ruled the Roman Empire for 23 years, spending the last eleven almost entirely outside Rome. Despite his gloomy reputation and difficult relationship with the Senate, Tiberius left the empire stable and the treasury full through careful fiscal management. He was succeeded by his grand-nephew and adopted grandson Caligula, who quickly drained the wealth Tiberius had accumulated. Tiberius received a sumptuous funeral but, unlike Augustus, was denied divine honors.
